conditions.name: Tobacco use disorder
conditions.overview: Study adult cigarette-smoking cessation, combined treatment and pregnancy-specific counseling. Medication decisions for children or other nicotine products are outside this module.

sources.title: Clinical Interventions to Treat Tobacco Use and Dependence Among Adults
sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.edition: Current clinician recommendations; page displays May 14 and May 15, 2024 dates
sources.locator: For non-pregnant patients: combining treatments; For pregnant patients; Follow up with patients

sources.title: Clinical Interventions to Treat Tobacco Use and Dependence Among Adults
sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.edition: CDC page displays May 14 and May 15, 2024 dates
sources.locator: For non-pregnant patients — Combining treatments; E-cigarettes and pregnancy
sources.limitations: CDC-authored adult cessation guidance. No medication doses or blanket pregnancy medication safety claims; the conflicting displayed day dates are not resolved by inventing one.

sections.title: Combine effective approaches
sections.text: For nonpregnant adult smokers, counseling plus an appropriate FDA-approved cessation medication improves success; combined long- and short-acting NRT is another supported strategy.

sections.title: Start with pregnancy counseling
sections.text: Pregnant smokers should first receive behavioral counseling and support. Medication benefits and harms need individualized assessment; e-cigarettes are not a safe pregnancy substitute.

sections.title: Support repeated attempts
sections.text: Tobacco dependence can relapse. Follow progress, address triggers and adjust treatment rather than withdrawing support after an unsuccessful attempt.

sections.title: Pair long- and short-acting nicotine replacement
sections.text: For suitable nonpregnant adults, CDC supports combining a long-acting nicotine patch with short-acting NRT such as gum or lozenges. The page states this improves quit success. Selection still requires individual suitability; this does not establish a pregnancy recommendation or specific dose. Varenicline and bupropion are separate prescription cessation medicines listed alongside NRT; they are not the short-acting NRT products in this combination.

sections.title: E-cigarettes are not a safe pregnancy cessation substitute
sections.text: CDC says e-cigarettes are not safe during pregnancy, are not FDA-approved smoking-cessation aids and lack sufficient evidence to establish smoking-cessation benefit. Behavioral counseling and support are the initial pregnancy approach; medication decisions require individualized benefit–harm consideration.
sections.sourceLocator: For pregnant patients; E-cigarettes and pregnancy.

questions.stem: A nonpregnant adult smoker wants to quit after several unsuccessful attempts. Medication contraindications have been reviewed. Which plan best uses the CDC-supported combination approach?

choices.text: Wait until smoking causes symptomatic disease
Use chronic benzodiazepines for cessation
Offer counseling plus an appropriate FDA-approved cessation medication
Rely only on willpower without follow-up
Stop discussing cessation after previous failures

questions.explanation: Counseling and cessation medication work better together.

distractorExplanations.A: Delay misses effective treatment.
distractorExplanations.B: This is not a cessation regimen.
distractorExplanations.D: It omits the supported combination.
distractorExplanations.E: Repeated attempts warrant support.

questions.learningObjective: Select combined counseling and medication for adult smoking cessation.

questions.stem: A pregnant patient who smokes wants to begin a quit attempt and has received no cessation treatment. Which initial approach follows CDC guidance?

choices.text: Automatically prescribe varenicline to every pregnant smoker
Recommend e-cigarettes as a universally safe alternative
Defer quitting until after delivery
Ignore smoking if cigarette use is intermittent
Offer behavioral counseling and social support

questions.explanation: Pregnancy guidance starts with behavioral support; medication needs individualized consideration.

distractorExplanations.A: Medication is not an automatic pregnancy choice.
distractorExplanations.B: E-cigarettes are unsafe in pregnancy.
distractorExplanations.C: Earlier cessation has benefits.
distractorExplanations.D: Tobacco use still warrants intervention.

questions.learningObjective: Apply pregnancy-specific smoking cessation counseling.

questions.stem: A fictional nonpregnant adult is receiving counseling and tolerates a nicotine patch, but wants a source-supported nicotine-replacement combination. Contraindications have been assessed. Which combination matches CDC guidance?

choices.text: Varenicline plus bupropion
A nicotine patch plus varenicline
A long-acting nicotine patch plus short-acting nicotine gum or lozenges
Bupropion alone
Varenicline alone

questions.explanation: CDC supports combined long- and short-acting NRT for suitable nonpregnant adults; the question does not set doses or remove individual screening.

distractorExplanations.A: These are separate prescription cessation medicines, not the specified long- and short-acting NRT pair.
distractorExplanations.B: Varenicline is not the short-acting NRT product in the requested source-supported NRT combination.
distractorExplanations.D: This is a single prescription cessation medicine, not combined long- and short-acting NRT.
distractorExplanations.E: This is a single prescription cessation medicine, not the requested NRT combination.

questions.learningObjective: Identify a supported long- and short-acting NRT combination without extending it to pregnancy.

questions.stem: A fictional pregnant smoker asks whether switching to e-cigarettes is a safe, FDA-approved smoking-cessation treatment. Which counseling best reflects CDC's evidence and safety statements?

choices.text: Explain that e-cigarettes are not safe during pregnancy or FDA-approved cessation aids; offer behavioral support
Recommend e-cigarettes first because they do not burn tobacco
Postpone all cessation support until after delivery
Present vaping as an FDA-approved smoking-cessation medicine
Recommend vaping instead of counseling because cessation benefit is established

questions.explanation: CDC rejects e-cigarettes as a safe pregnancy substitute and notes their unapproved cessation status and uncertain cessation benefit. Behavioral counseling/support is the initial pregnancy approach.

distractorExplanations.B: CDC still states that e-cigarettes are not safe in pregnancy; lack of combustion does not establish the proposed safety claim.
distractorExplanations.C: CDC recommends behavioral counseling and support during pregnancy.
distractorExplanations.D: FDA cessation approval is not established by the source; CDC explicitly says e-cigarettes are not approved cessation aids.
distractorExplanations.E: CDC describes insufficient cessation evidence and recommends behavioral support.

questions.learningObjective: Communicate e-cigarette pregnancy safety and cessation-evidence limits accurately.

conditions.name: Acute epididymitis
conditions.overview: Study acute scrotal assessment, pathogen-risk-specific adult antibiotic regimens, partner care and response reassessment. Dose vignettes assume normal renal function and no relevant contraindication; renal adjustment, pediatric regimens, chronic orchialgia and uncommon etiologies remain outside scope.

sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

Original study paraphrases only; CDC originals are freely available. Attribution does not imply endorsement by CDC, HHS or the U.S. Government. No linked third-party work, figure, logo or full source document is imported.

sections.title: Exclude the time-sensitive emergency
sections.text: Sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain, especially without infection evidence, requires immediate urologic assessment for testicular torsion.

sections.title: Test the likely pathogens
sections.text: Suspected acute epididymitis warrants chlamydia/gonorrhea NAAT and a bacterial urine culture; treatment selection depends on STI and enteric-organism risk.

sections.title: Reassess nonresponse
sections.text: Symptoms not improving within 72 hours require reevaluation of diagnosis and treatment. Persistent swelling after treatment also warrants alternative-cause assessment.

sections.title: Negative ultrasound does not exclude epididymitis
sections.text: CDC says ultrasound is primarily used to evaluate possible spermatic-cord torsion in painful unilateral swelling. A negative ultrasound does not rule out epididymitis and does not by itself change its management. Clinical history, examination and objective inflammation/pathogen assessment remain important. Torsion that is not excluded still requires appropriate clinical evaluation.
sections.sourceLocator: Diagnostic Considerations, ultrasound-role and negative-ultrasound paragraphs.

sections.title: Cover STI and enteric risks when both are plausible
sections.text: For acute epididymitis likely due to chlamydia, gonorrhea or enteric organisms in a man who practices insertive anal sex, CDC lists ceftriaxone plus levofloxacin. Presumptive therapy is selected from pathogen-risk context before all results return. Levofloxacin monotherapy is reserved for likely enteric-only infection after source-defined exclusion of gonorrhea, not every case with possible enteric exposure. CDC separately lists ceftriaxone plus doxycycline for likely chlamydia/gonorrhea without the combined enteric-risk category.
sections.sourceLocator: Treatment — presumptive therapy; Recommended Regimens — likely chlamydia/gonorrhea, combined STI/enteric risk and enteric-only monotherapy conditions.

sections.title: STI regimen is a 10-day combination
sections.text: For acute epididymitis most likely caused by chlamydia or gonorrhea, CDC specifies ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 10 days. At 150 kg or more, the ceftriaxone dose is 1 g once. The doxycycline duration differs from uncomplicated chlamydia.
sections.sourceLocator: Treatment — first Recommended Regimen and weight footnote.

sections.title: Combined risk versus enteric-only treatment
sections.text: For STI plus enteric risk associated with insertive anal sex, use ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once (1 g at 150 kg or more) plus levofloxacin 500 mg orally daily for 10 days. Enteric-only levofloxacin monotherapy uses the same daily dose/duration, but requires gonorrhea ruled out by Gram, MB or GV stain assessment; bacterial culture and susceptibilities guide treatment.
sections.sourceLocator: Treatment — second and third Recommended Regimens; weight footnote and monotherapy-qualification paragraph.

sections.title: An allergy alternative needs consultation
sections.text: Alternative epididymitis regimens have not been studied in the CDC chapter; if an alternative is required because of drug allergy or intolerance, consult an infectious-disease specialist. Do not automatically transfer a gonorrhea-only alternative to epididymitis.
sections.sourceLocator: Special Considerations — Drug Allergy, Intolerance, and Adverse Reactions.

sections.title: Persistent swelling after therapy
sections.text: Pain can take weeks to fully resolve, but persistent swelling and tenderness after completing antimicrobial treatment requires assessment for alternative diagnoses such as tumor, abscess, infarction, testicular cancer, tuberculosis or fungal infection. Lack of improvement within 72 hours separately requires earlier reassessment.

questions.stem: A 19-year-old develops sudden severe unilateral scrotal pain. Testing does not support urethritis or a urinary infection, and the epididymitis diagnosis is uncertain. What is the priority?

choices.text: Immediate urologic evaluation for testicular torsion
Wait three days to assess antibiotic response
Routine follow-up in one month
Assume epididymitis from age alone
Treat only with an analgesic and dismiss the pain

questions.explanation: This presentation requires urgent torsion assessment.

distractorExplanations.B: Delay risks testicular viability.
distractorExplanations.C: The evaluation is time-sensitive.
distractorExplanations.D: Age alone cannot establish the diagnosis.
distractorExplanations.E: Analgesia does not resolve the diagnostic emergency.

questions.learningObjective: Prioritize torsion evaluation in sudden severe scrotal pain.

questions.stem: A patient treated for acute epididymitis reports no symptom improvement after three days. Which next step follows CDC guidance?

choices.text: Continue indefinitely without reassessment
Assume persistent symptoms prove cure
Stop all follow-up because antibiotics were prescribed
Reevaluate the diagnosis and treatment
Delay reassessment for several months

questions.explanation: Three-day nonresponse calls for diagnostic and treatment reassessment.

distractorExplanations.A: It ignores the nonresponse threshold.
distractorExplanations.B: Persistent symptoms do not prove cure.
distractorExplanations.C: Prescription alone does not establish response.
distractorExplanations.E: This exceeds the recommended reassessment interval.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize when epididymitis nonresponse needs reevaluation.

questions.stem: A fictional adult has a clinical presentation and objective inflammatory findings consistent with acute epididymitis. Appropriate evaluation has addressed concern for torsion. A scrotal ultrasound is negative. Which interpretation follows CDC guidance?

choices.text: Stop the epididymitis assessment because the ultrasound is normal
Let the normal scan override the objective inflammatory findings
Use the scan alone to distinguish STI organisms from enteric organisms
A negative ultrasound does not rule out epididymitis or independently negate the clinical assessment
Use the negative scan as the sole basis for dismissing any unresolved torsion concern

questions.explanation: CDC notes the limited diagnostic usefulness of ultrasound in clinically consistent epididymitis and explicitly states that a negative scan does not rule it out. Ongoing torsion concern still requires clinical evaluation.

distractorExplanations.A: CDC says a negative ultrasound does not rule out epididymitis.
distractorExplanations.B: The source retains clinical and objective assessment despite a negative scan.
distractorExplanations.C: Ultrasound does not replace the source's pathogen testing and clinical-risk assessment.
distractorExplanations.E: CDC emphasizes clinical evaluation when torsion is not otherwise excluded.

questions.learningObjective: Avoid using a negative ultrasound as an exclusion test for clinically supported epididymitis.

questions.stem: A fictional adult man has acute epididymitis and reports insertive anal sex. Chlamydia, gonorrhea and enteric organisms are plausible; gonorrhea has not been ruled out. No relevant drug contraindications are present. Which presumptive regimen matches the CDC combined-risk recommendation, without specifying doses?

choices.text: Levofloxacin alone
Ceftriaxone plus doxycycline
Ceftriaxone alone
Doxycycline alone
Ceftriaxone plus levofloxacin

questions.explanation: CDC lists this pair for acute epididymitis with possible STI and enteric causes in men who practice insertive anal sex. Enteric-only levofloxacin monotherapy requires the source's gonorrhea-exclusion condition.

distractorExplanations.A: The enteric-only monotherapy pathway requires gonorrhea to be ruled out; that condition is absent here.
distractorExplanations.B: CDC lists this pair for likely chlamydia/gonorrhea; its combined STI/enteric-risk category specifies ceftriaxone plus levofloxacin.
distractorExplanations.C: This omits the additional agent in CDC's combined STI/enteric-risk regimen.
distractorExplanations.D: This is not the combined STI/enteric-risk regimen in the source.

questions.learningObjective: Match combined STI/enteric epididymitis risk to the source regimen without an unsupported monotherapy shortcut.

questions.stem: A 70-kg adult man has acute epididymitis most likely caused by chlamydia or gonorrhea, without the combined enteric-risk context. Torsion has been appropriately assessed. Renal function is normal, and no relevant drug contraindication is present. Which regimen matches CDC guidance?

choices.text: Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days
Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 10 days alone
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 10 days
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once alone
Ceftriaxone 250 mg IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for 10 days

questions.explanation: The STI epididymitis regimen combines ceftriaxone with 10 days of doxycycline.

distractorExplanations.A: This substitutes the uncomplicated-chlamydia duration for the 10-day epididymitis course.
distractorExplanations.B: This omits ceftriaxone from the likely-STI combination.
distractorExplanations.D: This omits the 10-day doxycycline component.
distractorExplanations.E: The chapter specifies ceftriaxone 500 mg below 150 kg.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish the STI epididymitis combination and duration from uncomplicated chlamydia.

questions.stem: An adult develops acute epididymitis after urinary instrumentation. Enteric-only infection is judged most likely; urethral Gram-stain assessment has ruled out gonorrhea, and the bacterial isolate is susceptible to levofloxacin. Torsion is excluded, renal function is normal and there are no drug contraindications. Which listed regimen fits CDC's qualified monotherapy pathway?

choices.text: Levofloxacin 500 mg orally daily for 10 days
Levofloxacin 500 mg orally once as the complete course
Levofloxacin 500 mg orally daily for 7 days
Doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 10 days alone
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once alone

questions.explanation: The source-qualified enteric-only regimen is levofloxacin 500 mg daily for 10 days, guided by culture and susceptibility.

distractorExplanations.B: CDC specifies a 10-day course, not one dose.
distractorExplanations.C: The epididymitis course is 10 days.
distractorExplanations.D: This is not the listed enteric-only regimen.
distractorExplanations.E: This omits the source-specified enteric-only course.

questions.learningObjective: Select enteric-only epididymitis treatment only after the required pathogen assessment.

questions.stem: A 160-kg adult man has acute epididymitis after insertive anal sex, with possible STI and enteric causes. Gonorrhea is not excluded. Torsion has been assessed; renal function is normal and there are no relevant drug contraindications. Which regimen fits the combined-risk and weight recommendations?

choices.text: Levofloxacin 500 mg orally daily for 10 days alone
Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM once plus levofloxacin 500 mg orally daily for 10 days
Ceftriaxone 1 g IM once plus doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 10 days
Ceftriaxone 1 g IM once plus levofloxacin 500 mg orally daily for 10 days
Ceftriaxone 1 g IM once plus levofloxacin 500 mg orally once

questions.explanation: Combined risk calls for ceftriaxone plus a 10-day levofloxacin course; weight at least 150 kg increases ceftriaxone to 1 g.

distractorExplanations.A: Monotherapy does not satisfy the unexcluded-gonorrhea combined-risk pathway.
distractorExplanations.B: The ceftriaxone dose must be 1 g at this weight.
distractorExplanations.C: The combined STI/enteric-risk category specifies levofloxacin rather than the STI-only doxycycline pair.
distractorExplanations.E: The levofloxacin component is daily for 10 days, not one dose.

questions.learningObjective: Combine pathogen-risk category, weight threshold and duration in acute epididymitis.

questions.stem: An adult with likely STI-related acute epididymitis cannot receive the recommended combination because of a documented severe drug reaction. Which next step is supported by CDC rather than an assumed substitute regimen?

choices.text: Automatically prescribe the uncomplicated gonorrhea allergy regimen as a validated epididymitis substitute
Consult an infectious-disease specialist because alternative epididymitis regimens have not been studied
Use any single oral antibiotic regardless of pathogen risk
Omit antibiotic treatment because an allergy is present
Use an enteric-only regimen despite unexcluded gonorrhea

questions.explanation: CDC recommends consultation when an alternative epididymitis regimen is needed.

distractorExplanations.A: The chapter does not validate transferring gonorrhea-only alternatives to epididymitis.
distractorExplanations.C: Selection depends on pathogens and contraindications, not any available oral agent.
distractorExplanations.D: An allergy requires an alternative-treatment assessment, not abandonment of indicated treatment.
distractorExplanations.E: The enteric-only pathway requires gonorrhea exclusion.

questions.learningObjective: Recognize when drug intolerance requires expert-guided epididymitis treatment.

questions.stem: An adult completed the prescribed acute epididymitis antimicrobial course. Although pain improved initially, focal swelling and tenderness remain. Which next step follows CDC's postcourse follow-up guidance?

choices.text: Assume complete cure from completion of antibiotics alone
Repeat the same antibiotic indefinitely without reassessing the diagnosis
Treat persistent swelling as proof of gonorrhea resistance
Dismiss the findings because pain may take weeks to resolve
Evaluate for alternative diagnoses such as tumor, abscess or infarction

questions.explanation: Persistent swelling/tenderness after treatment warrants alternative-diagnosis assessment even though discomfort can resolve slowly.

distractorExplanations.A: Course completion does not remove the need to assess persistent swelling.
distractorExplanations.B: CDC specifies reassessment rather than indefinite repetition.
distractorExplanations.C: Persistent swelling is not itself proof of a particular resistant pathogen.
distractorExplanations.D: Slow pain resolution does not negate the separate postcourse swelling recommendation.

questions.learningObjective: Separate slow symptom recovery from persistent findings requiring diagnostic reassessment.

conditions.name: Scabies
conditions.overview: Study prescribed scabicide selection and the distinction between classic and crusted scabies. Household outbreak protocols and exact application schedules require separate guidance.

sources.title: Clinical Care of Scabies
sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.locator: Classic scabies: first-line medications; Crusted scabies: oral and topical agents

sources.title: Clinical Care of Scabies
sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.locator: Classic scabies — oral ivermectin safety boundaries
sources.limitations: No ivermectin dose or claim of established pregnancy safety; oral ivermectin is not FDA-approved for scabies. Source-defined lack of safety data is distinct from a universal contraindication.

sources.title: Preventing Scabies
sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.locator: Overview — simultaneous household/close-contact treatment and clothing/bedding measures
sources.limitations: Human scabies household prevention only; no pesticide fumigation, veterinary extrapolation or copied images.

sections.title: Treat classic infestation
sections.text: Permethrin 5% cream is a first-line classic-scabies option, FDA-approved from age two months. Additional applications may be needed.

sections.title: Respect oral-treatment boundaries
sections.text: Oral ivermectin is an alternative for classic scabies but is not FDA-approved for that indication; safety is unestablished in pregnancy and children under 15 kg.

sections.title: Use combined crusted-scabies treatment
sections.text: Crusted scabies requires oral plus topical treatment; intensive schedules vary with severity and should not be borrowed from uncomplicated cases.

sections.title: Do not invent established oral-ivermectin safety
sections.text: CDC states that oral ivermectin is not FDA-approved for scabies treatment and that its safety in pregnancy and children weighing less than 15 kg has not been established. This is a safety-evidence boundary, not permission to label the drug established safe for those groups or to invent a dosing workaround.
sections.sourceLocator: Classic scabies — Ivermectin oral tablet bullet.

sections.title: Treat household contacts together
sections.text: CDC recommends treating household members and close contacts at the same time as the person with scabies, and washing clothing and bedding used during the 3 days before treatment. Appropriate laundering or isolation of unwashable items is part of spread control. Do not wait for each household member to develop symptoms before applying the source's simultaneous-treatment approach.
sections.sourceLocator: Overview — simultaneous treatment and clothing/bedding bullets.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old has confirmed classic scabies without crusting or contraindications. Which listed topical treatment is a CDC first-line option?

choices.text: Topical acyclovir
Permethrin 5% cream
An oral antibiotic alone
Hydrocortisone alone
A topical antifungal alone

questions.explanation: Permethrin 5% is a first-line scabicide for this age.

distractorExplanations.A: It does not kill scabies mites.
distractorExplanations.C: Antibiotics do not eradicate the infestation.
distractorExplanations.D: Steroid alone is not scabicidal treatment.
distractorExplanations.E: This does not target scabies mites.

questions.learningObjective: Choose a supported topical treatment for classic scabies.

questions.stem: A transplant recipient has confirmed crusted scabies. Oral and topical agents are suitable, and specialists are organizing treatment. Which medication strategy matches CDC guidance?

choices.text: Use only an antihistamine
Use a routine topical steroid as definitive therapy
Combine an oral agent with a topical scabicide
Always use a single topical application alone
Avoid treating until itching becomes intense

questions.explanation: Crusted infestation calls for combined oral and topical treatment.

distractorExplanations.A: Symptom relief does not eradicate mites.
distractorExplanations.B: It is not definitive scabicidal treatment.
distractorExplanations.D: Crusted disease needs a different regimen.
distractorExplanations.E: Treatment should not wait for itching.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish crusted-scabies treatment from classic-scabies therapy.

questions.stem: A fictional pregnant adult with classic scabies asks whether oral ivermectin has established pregnancy safety. Which statement preserves the CDC evidence boundary?

choices.text: Select oral ivermectin from adult classic-scabies efficacy data without a pregnancy safety review
Safety of oral ivermectin in pregnancy has not been established; discuss suitable options rather than promise safety
Treat off-label scabies use as evidence of FDA-approved pregnancy safety
Use the adult's weight above 15 kg as the only safety consideration
Transfer topical-treatment safety assumptions directly to the oral drug

questions.explanation: CDC describes unestablished pregnancy safety and unapproved US scabies indication for oral ivermectin. Lack of established safety must not be rewritten as a guarantee of safety.

distractorExplanations.A: The source's ordinary efficacy statement does not remove the specific pregnancy safety gap.
distractorExplanations.C: Oral ivermectin is not FDA-approved for scabies, and its pregnancy safety is not established.
distractorExplanations.D: The under-15-kg caution concerns children; the separate pregnancy safety gap still applies.
distractorExplanations.E: CDC describes an oral-ivermectin-specific safety limitation that cannot be filled by another formulation's assumptions.

questions.learningObjective: Preserve an oral-ivermectin pregnancy safety gap without inventing approval or safety.

questions.stem: In a fictional household, one person has confirmed scabies and other close contacts have no current itch. Which control plan follows CDC guidance?

choices.text: Treat symptomatic members now and wait for symptoms in the other close contacts
Treat only the bed-sharing contact and omit other household members
Arrange simultaneous treatment of household members and close contacts, with the recommended clothing/bedding measures
Treat household members sequentially over several weeks
Arrange simultaneous contact treatment but defer clothing and bedding measures until recurrence

questions.explanation: CDC recommends treating household members and close contacts at the same time as the infected person. The source also addresses items used in the 3 days before treatment.

distractorExplanations.A: CDC recommends simultaneous treatment of household members and close contacts.
distractorExplanations.B: The source includes household members and close contacts, not only one bed-sharing contact.
distractorExplanations.D: Sequential treatment does not implement the source's simultaneous approach.
distractorExplanations.E: The source includes items used in the 3 days before treatment, rather than waiting for recurrence.

questions.learningObjective: Use simultaneous household scabies control rather than symptom-by-symptom delay.

conditions.name: Pediculosis capitis
conditions.overview: Study head-lice treatment timing, persistent infestation and medication precautions. School-exclusion policies and diagnostic nit interpretation are outside this module.

sources.title: Clinical Care of Head Lice
sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.locator: Permethrin 1%; prescription alternatives; malathion precautions; treatment precautions

sources.title: Treatment of Head Lice
sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.locator: Directions — slow lice at 8–12 hours; Treatment overview; Additional measures — avoid fumigants; Treatment issues — mayonnaise evidence
sources.limitations: Head lice only. No extrapolation to scabies or pubic lice; no insecticide doses, excessive retreatment or veterinary product instructions.

sections.title: Account for surviving eggs
sections.text: Permethrin 1% kills live lice but not unhatched eggs; a repeat treatment around day nine may be needed.

sections.title: Reassess persistent crawling lice
sections.text: Live lice after a complete treatment and retreatment course can justify another medication; incorrect use and resistance can reduce effectiveness.

sections.title: Use malathion safely
sections.text: Malathion lotion is flammable. Avoid smoking and electrical heat sources during application and while hair remains wet.

sections.title: Do not equate slow early movement with treatment failure
sections.text: CDC says that a few lice moving slowly 8–12 hours after treatment do not require immediate reapplication; medication can take time to kill lice. If no lice have died and they remain as active as before treatment at that time, discuss possible failure with the provider before retreatment. Follow the medication's actual retreatment instructions.

sections.title: Avoid environmental fumigant sprays and fogs
sections.text: CDC advises against fumigant sprays or fogs for head-lice control because they can be toxic if inhaled or absorbed through skin. Suggested additional measures include laundering appropriate recently used items and vacuuming. Environmental pesticide exposure is not a substitute for correct treatment of an active infestation. Animals do not get or spread head lice. CDC also reports no scientific evidence that mayonnaise or similar suffocating substances effectively treat head lice.
sections.sourceLocator: Treatment overview; Additional measures — laundering/vacuuming and no-fumigant bullets; Treatment issues — mayonnaise evidence statement.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old with confirmed head lice receives permethrin 1%. The family asks why instructions may include another treatment around day nine. Which explanation is correct?

choices.text: Every lice medicine kills all eggs immediately
The repeat treatment is for fungal infection
Permethrin is only an antibiotic
Repeat treatment should always occur hourly
Unhatched eggs survive, so newly hatched lice may need treatment

questions.explanation: Permethrin does not kill unhatched eggs.

distractorExplanations.A: Ovicidal activity differs by agent.
distractorExplanations.B: The target remains lice.
distractorExplanations.C: Permethrin is a pediculicide.
distractorExplanations.D: Hourly use is inappropriate overuse.

questions.learningObjective: Explain why a nonovicidal lice treatment may need repetition.

questions.stem: An adult applies prescribed malathion lotion for head lice and wants to dry the wet hair with a heated hair dryer. What counseling is appropriate?

choices.text: Avoid the dryer and other ignition sources because malathion is flammable
Use maximum dryer heat to improve treatment
Smoke while waiting for the lotion to dry
Mix several lice medicines without instructions
Apply extra lotion continuously until hair dries

questions.explanation: Malathion requires avoidance of heat and ignition sources while wet.

distractorExplanations.B: Heat creates a fire hazard.
distractorExplanations.C: Smoking creates an ignition source.
distractorExplanations.D: Unsupervised combinations are discouraged.
distractorExplanations.E: Extra medication risks misuse.

questions.learningObjective: Prevent a malathion-related ignition hazard.

questions.stem: In a fictional head-lice treatment follow-up, a parent sees only a few lice moving slowly 10 hours after medication application. They ask whether to immediately apply another full treatment. Which response best follows CDC instructions?

choices.text: Do not immediately reapply solely for slow movement at 8–12 hours; follow the medication instructions and remove remaining lice appropriately
Repeat the full application now rather than wait for the product-directed interval
Switch to another medication immediately because slow movement establishes failure
Use more of the current product than the instructions specify to speed killing
Treat slow movement as confirmed resistance requiring a medication change

questions.explanation: CDC explains that some lice can move slowly early after treatment while medication takes effect. This differs from lice remaining fully active without evidence of killing.

distractorExplanations.B: Slow movement at 8–12 hours does not by itself call for immediate reapplication.
distractorExplanations.C: CDC distinguishes slowly moving lice from lice remaining fully active, and does not establish failure from this early finding.
distractorExplanations.D: CDC directs using medication as instructed; the source does not authorize an extra amount for slow early movement.
distractorExplanations.E: The stated early response does not prove resistance.

questions.learningObjective: Distinguish early slow lice movement from immediate treatment failure.

questions.stem: A fictional family treating a confirmed head-lice infestation proposes using pesticide foggers throughout the home. What source-supported environmental advice should be given?

choices.text: Fog the rooms after laundering to eliminate environmental lice
Treat the family pet as the reservoir instead of addressing the infestation
Use mayonnaise as a proven substitute for indicated infestation treatment
Avoid fumigant sprays or fogs; use appropriate laundering and vacuuming measures instead
Spray fumigant on bedding as a safer substitute for laundry

questions.explanation: CDC warns that fumigant sprays and fogs can be toxic if inhaled or absorbed through skin and recommends other limited environmental measures.

distractorExplanations.A: CDC specifically advises against fumigant sprays and fogs because of toxicity.
distractorExplanations.B: The source states that animals do not get or spread head lice.
distractorExplanations.C: CDC reports no scientific evidence that this suffocating approach is effective.
distractorExplanations.E: Changing the target surface does not remove the source's warning against fumigants.

questions.learningObjective: Choose safer limited environmental head-lice control rather than toxic fumigation.

conditions.name: Tinea corporis
conditions.overview: Study body-ringworm recognition, diagnostic confirmation and antifungal stewardship. Scalp/nail infection, resistant-strain regimens and exact antifungal doses are outside this module.

sources.title: Clinical Overview of Ringworm
sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.locator: Skin infections; avoid corticosteroid creams; testing and diagnosis

sources.title: Clinical Treatment of Fungal Diseases: Antifungals
sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.locator: Appropriate use: topical antifungals and topical corticosteroids

sources.title: Treatment of Ringworm
sources.organization: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
sources.locator: Treatment types — Ringworm on the skin; Emerging and severe antifungal-resistant ringworm
sources.limitations: This general skin-treatment summary is not a regimen for scalp, nail or invasive fungal infection. Failure prompts evaluation; it does not prove resistance or select a drug by travel history alone.

sections.title: Recognize the possible pattern
sections.text: An expanding scaly ring with central clearing suggests dermatophyte infection; eczema and other rashes can resemble ringworm.

sections.title: Confirm before prescribing
sections.text: CDC recommends testing suspected fungal skin infection before prescribing treatment when feasible, rather than relying on appearance alone.

sections.title: Avoid steroid combinations
sections.text: For fungal skin infection, use antifungals without corticosteroids whenever possible; steroid-containing combinations can worsen infection and promote treatment problems.

sections.title: Treat skin disease for the directed course
sections.text: CDC describes ringworm on the skin as usually treated with nonprescription topical antifungals, commonly for 2–4 weeks according to product instructions. Apply treatment for the directed duration even if symptoms improve. This skin-treatment approach must not be automatically substituted for scalp ringworm, which generally requires oral prescription treatment.
sections.sourceLocator: Treatment types — Ringworm on the skin and Ringworm on the scalp.

sections.title: Persistent or widespread disease needs reassessment
sections.text: CDC advises health care evaluation for ringworm that is unusually severe or widespread, persists after treatment or follows contact with severe infection. Report relevant travel history. Emerging resistant disease may not respond to usual antifungals, but persistence or travel alone does not prove resistance or establish a specific alternative regimen.
sections.sourceLocator: Emerging and severe antifungal-resistant ringworm; When to contact a healthcare provider.

questions.stem: An adult has an expanding scaly annular forearm lesion with central clearing. Ringworm and eczema are being considered, and diagnostic testing is available. What best follows CDC clinician guidance before prescribing?

choices.text: Assume all annular lesions are eczema
Start a potent steroid without assessing infection
Treat the appearance as proof without testing
Obtain diagnostic testing for fungal infection
Prescribe an antibiotic for every annular lesion

questions.explanation: Testing helps distinguish ringworm from mimicking conditions.

distractorExplanations.A: Appearance alone is insufficient.
distractorExplanations.B: Steroids can worsen ringworm.
distractorExplanations.C: CDC recommends diagnostic confirmation.
distractorExplanations.E: No bacterial diagnosis is established.

questions.learningObjective: Use diagnostic confirmation for a rash that may be tinea corporis.

questions.stem: A patient has confirmed tinea corporis. A colleague proposes a topical antifungal combined with a high-potency corticosteroid. Which response reflects CDC stewardship guidance?

choices.text: Use the steroid combination because steroids eradicate dermatophytes
Choose an appropriate antifungal without a steroid whenever possible
Replace all antifungal treatment with prednisone
Assume a stronger steroid always shortens treatment
Treat only itch and ignore fungal persistence

questions.explanation: Steroid-containing combinations can worsen fungal skin infection.

distractorExplanations.A: Steroids are not antifungal therapy.
distractorExplanations.C: Prednisone does not eradicate dermatophytes.
distractorExplanations.D: Steroids can prolong treatment problems.
distractorExplanations.E: Symptom relief is not eradication.

questions.learningObjective: Avoid unnecessary corticosteroids in dermatophyte treatment.

questions.stem: A fictional adult has confirmed localized tinea corporis and no relevant drug contraindication. Symptoms improve after several days of an appropriate topical antifungal. Which instruction follows CDC's skin-ringworm guidance?

choices.text: Stop the antifungal once itch improves even if the directed course is unfinished
Switch to an oral antifungal solely because symptoms are improving
Replace the antifungal with a topical steroid as maintenance for residual redness
Apply the antifungal only on days with visible symptoms rather than follow instructions
Continue the topical antifungal for the product-directed duration even when symptoms improve

questions.explanation: CDC advises using skin antifungal treatment for as long as directed, commonly 2–4 weeks depending on the product. Early symptom improvement is not the sole stopping rule.

distractorExplanations.A: CDC says to apply the antifungal for as long as directed, despite early improvement.
distractorExplanations.B: The described response does not replace the source's instruction to complete appropriate directed skin treatment.
distractorExplanations.C: This replaces the antifungal rather than completing the product-directed course described by CDC.
distractorExplanations.D: Intermittent symptom-triggered use does not implement the directed course in this vignette.

questions.learningObjective: Retain the directed topical course after early improvement in confirmed skin ringworm.

questions.stem: A fictional adult develops extensive ringworm-like lesions that persist after correctly completed usual treatment following recent travel. What is the source-supported next step, without presuming resistance or choosing an unverified drug?

choices.text: Repeat the same course without discussing the persistent extensive disease
Seek reassessment and report severity, treatment response and travel history
Add a topical steroid to suppress the persistent rash
Assume travel proves resistance and choose a new regimen without reassessment
Dismiss a fungal cause solely from treatment nonresponse

questions.explanation: CDC recommends evaluation for severe/widespread or persistent disease and sharing travel history. Emerging resistant infections are a consideration, but the findings do not prove resistance.

distractorExplanations.A: Persistence or unusual extent is a source-listed reason for evaluation.
distractorExplanations.C: This does not provide the reassessment CDC recommends for persistent or unusually extensive disease.
distractorExplanations.D: Travel history informs assessment; it does not prove resistance or provide a regimen.
distractorExplanations.E: The source recommends reassessment, not a definitive alternate diagnosis from nonresponse alone.

questions.learningObjective: Reassess persistent extensive ringworm without fabricating resistance or an alternative regimen.
